extracted.intended_audience: academic researchers and legal scholars studying administrative law, agency rulemaking, and empirical political science
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical analysis of federal agency rulemaking: modeling initiation and completion of rulemakings using agency-level measures (capacity, independence, ideology, workload, contractors) and survival/OLS methods to test hypotheses about presidential control and capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity (policymaking capacity)
rubrics_metrics.description: A continuous measure of an agency’s policymaking capacity used as the primary independent variable predicting rulemaking completion and initiation. Capacity is measured at the start of the presidential administration and interpreted relative to the sample mean (e.g., one standard deviation above the mean = "high-capacity").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use capacity measured before the 'treatment' (start of the administration) to avoid post-treatment bias. Report effects in standardized terms (±1 SD) for interpretability (e.g., high-capacity agency is 57% more likely to complete an ongoing rulemaking). Consider interactions between capacity and measures of presidential control (independence, ideological distance). Capacity should not simply proxy workload; test correlations with other covariates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural independence (agency independence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure of agency independence derived from statutory design features (Selin’s 2015 measure of decision-maker independence), ranging from low to high (0.00 to 3.08 in Selin’s scale).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model independence as a continuous measure and also check robustness by substituting a binary indicator for independent commission. Interact independence with capacity to test Completion and Initiation Hypotheses. Be cautious where lack of variation (e.g., omission of highest-independence agencies) can impede estimation of interaction effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideological distance between agency and President
rubrics_metrics.description: A time-invariant measure of agency ideology (Richardson, Clinton & Lewis) constructed from surveys of federal executives about whether agencies slant liberal/conservative; transformed into ideological distance so conservative agencies are closest to Republican presidents and liberal agencies to Democratic presidents (range reported e.g., 0.06 to 3.94).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the time-invariant survey-based measure to avoid endogeneity from post-treatment politicization. Interact ideological distance with capacity to test whether the marginal effect of distance on duration/initiation decreases as capacity decreases. Acknowledge imprecision where estimates are statistically insignificant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workload (baseline rulemaking workload)
rubrics_metrics.description: Logged number of rulemakings reported in the Unified Agenda in the fall before a new President’s inauguration; intended to capture an agency’s baseline level of rulemaking activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Log-transform skewed counts before inclusion. Use this as a control for expected level of rulemaking activity so that capacity is not simply proxying workload. Check correlation with capacity (Pearson correlation) to assess multicollinearity concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contractors (proxy via contract managers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Logged number of contract managers employed full time by the agency used as a proxy for the agency’s reliance on contract services in rulemaking (raw range before log: 1 to 5,815 contract managers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because direct data on contracting for rulemaking is difficult to obtain, this is a crude proxy; test robustness by removing this measure. Report correlations with capacity and note insignificant correlations may reduce concern about confounding. Acknowledge measurement limitations and transparency problems in contractor data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'significant' rulemaking (dependent variable for initiation analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulemakings coded as 'significant' if reported as 'economically significant' or 'other significant' on the Unified Agenda. 'Economically significant' defined as having at least a $100 million annual effect on the economy (threshold raised to $200 million later, but not affecting the present analysis). 'Other significant' are those that are a priority of the agency head.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggregate significant NPRMs to the agency-term level for initiation analysis. Use this subset because they represent large policy initiatives likely prioritized by the White House. Note changes in federal thresholds over time and discuss whether they affect the sample.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent variable: time-to-rulemaking completion (duration analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use duration (time to completion/finalization of rulemakings) as the dependent variable, modeled with survival analysis (Cox proportional hazards model).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Cox model estimates both whether higher-capacity agencies complete rules before the end of a President’s first term and whether they complete rulemakings faster (hazard rates). Interpret positive coefficients as faster completion (higher hazard of finalization) and negative as longer durations. Use survival methods when timing matters and censoring is present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent variable: number of significant NPRMs (initiation analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Count of significant NPRMs initiated by an agency during a President’s first term (aggregated to agency-term); modeled using ordinary least squares (OLS) regression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive coefficients indicate initiation of more rulemakings; negative coefficients indicate fewer. Include the same agency-level controls as in duration models. Use OLS with heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors clustered at agency level as specified, and test robustness with alternative specifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modeling choices: interactions and fixed effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Include interaction terms between capacity and measures of presidential control (independence, ideological distance) and include fixed effects for presidential administrations to capture time-varying procedural or policy changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret interaction terms to assess whether marginal effects of control decline as capacity decreases. Use presidential fixed effects to control for administration-specific policies (e.g., Exec. Order 13,771). Avoid including post-treatment covariates or agency fixed effects when they would introduce bias or when insufficient within-agency variation prevents estimation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical inference and reporting conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use robust standard errors (e.g., R’s survival package robust SEs; HC1-type heteroskedastic-consistent SEs clustered at agency level), perform joint hypothesis tests using the Wald test, and report p-values with conventional star notation (*p < 0.10; **p < 0.05; ***p < 0.001).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report both statistical significance and discuss practical significance. Where interaction coefficients are statistically insignificant, acknowledge imprecision and avoid overinterpretation. Use appropriate clustering and heteroskedasticity-robust SEs for inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standardization and interpretation of unit changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Report effects in standardized terms (e.g., difference between agencies one standard deviation above vs below the mean) and clearly state what a one-SD change implies in substantive terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ±1 SD to define 'high' and 'low' categories for plotting and interpretation (e.g., 'high capacity' = +1 SD). Apply same convention to ideological distance and independence when plotting predicted functions. Hold other controls at their mean when plotting predicted hazards or counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformations for skewed variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply log transformations to skewed count variables (e.g., number of rulemakings, number of contract managers) prior to modeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain pre-transformation ranges and summary statistics. Use log transformation to reduce skewness and to interpret multiplicative effects. Note the meaning of logged values when interpreting coefficients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding post-treatment bias and endogeneity
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not include measures that could be affected by the 'treatment' (e.g., politicization measures measured after the start of an administration) because they can induce post-treatment bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define independent variables before the treatment (start of administration). If politicization or other time-varying measures are potentially endogenous, either omit them or use pre-treatment proxies. Cite Rosenbaum (1984) when discussing adjustment risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling insufficient within-unit variation (agency fixed effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not include agency fixed effects when agencies exhibit stability in the key independent variables across administrations and there is insufficient within-agency variation to identify effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain lack of variation and justify omission. If within-agency effects cannot be estimated reliably, rely on cross-sectional variation and include other controls/fixed effects (e.g., presidential fixed effects) instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of survey-based, time-invariant measures for ideology
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer stable, time-invariant measures constructed from surveys of federal executives for agency ideology to avoid contamination by current administration dynamics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transform survey responses as needed to align with partisan mappings. Justify time invariance and discuss limitations (e.g., potential measurement error).

rubrics_metrics.name: Robustness checks and alternative specifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Substitute alternative measures (e.g., Selin’s continuous independence measure vs a binary independent-commission indicator) and remove potentially crude proxies (e.g., contract managers) to test robustness of results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report that results hold under alternative specifications and report appendix robustness tables. Note where certain variables’ measurement limitations (e.g., contractors) do not change core findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations: scope of outcome and potential unobserved quality failures
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge that analyzing rulemaking completion does not capture all ways capacity affects policymaking (e.g., procedural defects leading to judicial vacatur or flawed technical analyses that produce poor substantive outcomes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss examples (e.g., EPA erroneous formula for safe consumption) demonstrating how capacity problems can produce substantive or procedural failures not reflected in completion time. Use this limitation to temper claims about capacity’s role and to motivate future work on quality and legal durability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of coefficients in duration and count models
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret positive coefficients in Cox models as indicating faster rulemaking (higher hazard of finalization) and positive coefficients in OLS as indicating initiation of more significant rulemakings; negative coefficients indicate the opposite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate coefficient magnitudes into substantive statements (e.g., a one-SD increase in capacity corresponds to a 57% greater likelihood of completion at any point in time, or about nine more significant NPRMs initiated). Distinguish statistical significance from practical importance and discuss uncertainty in interaction estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing for correlations and multicollinearity among covariates
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Pearson correlation tests (or other diagnostics) to evaluate relationships between covariates (e.g., capacity vs workload; capacity vs number of contract managers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report correlation coefficients and p-values to show whether measures proxy one another. Use these diagnostics to alleviate or flag concerns about confounding and multicollinearity.
